items.explanation: The burning buses and beaten riders of 1961 horrified the nation on TV — but neither Washington nor the states moved decisively to protect civil rights workers at that point.
options: A. Southerners had accepted integration orders
B. State governments enforced civil rights laws
C. Television news held a powerful grip on the public
D. Washington was committed to protecting civil rights

items.explanation: Tet was a Vietcong military disaster — but the images of fighting in Saigon and Hue proved official optimism ('victory around the corner') had been dishonest, shattering public trust.
options: A. America was near decisive victory
B. Officials had not been candid about the war
C. The Vietcong could beat Americans in battle
D. U.S.–South Vietnamese cooperation was improving

items.explanation: SDS peaked during the 1965–67 escalation, when the draft touched millions of students; by Cambodia (1970) and the 1972 bombing, it had splintered into factions.
options: A. The draft sent more young men to Vietnam, 1965–67
B. Southern civil rights struggles aired on TV
C. Nixon invaded Cambodia
D. Nixon's 1972 bombing peaked

items.explanation: Northern Blacks embraced Black Power as King's integrationism seemed distant, ghettos stayed poor, and Malcolm X and Carmichael offered pride — but only a small minority actually joined the Nation of Islam.
options: A. King seemed focused on the South, not the ghetto
B. Northern ghettos remained poor and hopeless
C. Malcolm X and Carmichael evoked Black pride
D. Vast numbers joined the Nation of Islam

items.explanation: Black Power rose precisely when legal victories — the Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts — had been won but had not changed ghetto life, shifting the demand from legal equality to economic and cultural power.
options: A. Government repression of free speech
B. Declining legal rights for Black Americans
C. Expanding legal rights for Black Americans
D. Economic depression in America
